text:
We called him Q because his actual name—Quentin Kensington—sounded like a nineteenth-century novel, and because in 2011, reducing a person to a single consonant felt like the height of undergraduate economy. He arrived at our New Haven dormitory with two leather valises, an unstrung squash racket, and a preternatural inability to experience social friction.

I was his roommate by algorithmic quirk. While I spent freshman year in a panic over how not to sound like a provincial clerk in seminars, Q existed in effortless calibration. He possessed a golden symmetry that flattered any room he entered. His linen shirts wrinkled in patterns suggesting leisure rather than neglect. In tutorials, he spoke of Thucydides as if they were boarding-school chums who had had a mild falling-out in Newport.

Every golden boy requires a Boswell to walk half a pace behind him, and I filled the role with fascinated passivity. I watched Q navigate our early twenties without scraping his hull. When he forgot a twenty-page paper until the night before it was due, he didn’t weep in Sterling Library; he went to the Elizabethan Club, smoked cloves with a visiting lecturer, and received an extension so open-ended I doubt he ever finished it.

With women, his grace was equally frictionless. Relationships dissolved into a nostalgic mist, leaving his partners convinced they had outgrown him, and that he was bravely stepping aside for their flourishing. "She needs Berlin right now," he told me once, eating an apple with a pocketknife while a girl named Clara wept in the stairwell. "Who am I to stand in the way of Berlin?"

After graduation, the drift was immediate. Q went to London, then to a boutique consulting firm whose website consisted solely of a compass and a Zurich telephone number. I moved to New York, working for preservation nonprofits. I rarely thought of him, except when required to exercise velvet-gloved ruthlessness—firing an intern, or telling a donor their grandfather’s terracotta gargoyles were poured concrete. *How would Q do this?* I would wonder, knowing Q would never be near fake gargoyles.

Ten years after graduation, on a Tuesday in July, I saw him at the Rockaway Bathing Club.

I was there on a guest pass from my friend Arthur, a newly divorced tax attorney. The club was an exercise in curated austerity: bleached cabanas and a saltwater pool absorbing the Atlantic glare. Feeling the humiliation of a faded J.Crew swimsuit among trunks engineered in Milan, I settled onto a lounger beneath an overhang with a Robert Moses biography and Arthur’s straw hat pulled low.

Then I heard the laugh: a soft intake of breath followed by three descending notes, like water poured from a pitcher.

Two loungers to my left, behind a planter of ornamental grasses, sat Q. Time had not ruined him, only thickened him slightly. His honey-colored hair had receded just enough to suggest gravitas, his shoulders gilded from Februaries in St. Barts. He wore rolled linen trousers and a translucent white polo.

Across from him, perched on her lounger, was a woman in her late twenties. She was dressed entirely wrong for the beach: a black blazer over a floral sundress, and loafers without socks—the uniform of a junior associate told "let's meet somewhere casual" who had panicked at dawn. A leather portfolio lay across her shins like a shield.

"The thing to understand about Antwerp," Q was saying, with that buttery tutorial-room cadence, "is that they don't view restructuring as subtraction. It’s an editorial process. A tightening of syntax."

"Right," the woman said, her voice brisk, anxious, and midwestern. "I understand the macro view, Quentin. I saw the redundancies in the Brussels-Antwerp corridor. I spent June learning the regulatory framework for Flemish municipal bonds and integrated the Ghent portfolio into my workflow."

She unzipped the portfolio with a metallic *zzt* and pulled out a stapled sheaf—making Q’s left eyelid flutter with aesthetic distress.

"Look," she said, leaning forward. "In column three, you’ll see the yield projections I ran last night. Even without support staff, my unit is operating fourteen percent above baseline. If the Zurich move depends on proving cross-border scalability—"

"Meredith," Q said. He didn't touch the paper, placing two fingers lightly on her portfolio, as if blessing a hound. "Nobody has ever questioned your numeracy. Good grief. With three more of you, we could close Frankfurt and run Europe out of a Basel flat."

He gave her the Kensington smile, designed to make the recipient feel they were the only two sentient beings in a bureaucratic world.

Meredith did not smile. "Then I don't understand why my name wasn't on the transition manifest this morning," she said, flat and clear. "Giles was on it. And Giles hasn't closed an institutional account since last year."

"Giles," Q said, adjusting his tortoiseshell sunglasses, "is a peculiar case. His uncle was on the board in '98. It’s less about what Giles *does*, and more about what his presence *signifies* to septuagenarians in Geneva."

"So I’m being passed over for Zurich because Giles has an uncle."

"No, God, no." Q laughed again. He planted his espadrilles on the concrete. Behind my reeds, I noticed something I had never seen in four years of sharing a dorm: a crescent of sweat beneath the armhole of his polo. "You’re thinking so linearly, Meredith. Zurich isn't a prize; it’s a salt mine. Compliance is suffocating. Someone with your instinct for the *human* texture of the work would wither there."

"I like Zurich," Meredith said. "My fiancé already applied for a transfer to Oerlikon. You knew that. You told him at the Christmas party which tram line to live near."

Silence fell. A waiter drifted past with lobster rolls, and Q watched him with an intensity bordering on longing.

"Did I?" Q murmured. He removed his sunglasses, polishing the lenses on his shirt. Without dark glass, his face looked unfinished, the skin beneath his eyes papery from too many pressurized cabins. "Yes, the four-line. Well, Meredith, the New York narrative has shifted. Algorithms will eat the Flemish bond market within eighteen months. What I’ve argued for, at some cost to my political capital, is to carve out a lateral space here. A roving domestic brief."

"There is no roving domestic brief," Meredith said. "We divested from the North American municipal sector in November. I wrote the press release."

Q stopped polishing his glasses. For three seconds, the mechanism jammed. I watched his jaw work as he searched the archive of his charm for a classical allusion or self-deprecating shrug that would dissolve this intractable woman into the warm mist where Clara lived.

Nothing came. He was thirty-two, sitting by a Rockaway pool, just a middle manager who hadn't read the briefing packet before firing someone.

"Well," Q said, his voice cracking. "The nomenclature is in flux."

"Are you letting me go, Quentin?"

"Nobody is using that language," he said quickly, staring through the planter grass toward my face, seeing only a corner he couldn't turn. "HR drafted something generous—six months base, keeping you on the consultancy roster through autumn so there’s no CV gap. Think of it as a runway."

"You made me take the A train out here," she said, sounding less angry than astonished, as if discovering a cathedral was made of styrofoam. "An hour from Fulton Street, in a blazer, to lay me off by a pool because you didn't want to do it in the conference room."

"I thought it would be more civilized," Q said, and for the first time in fourteen years, he sounded entirely sincere, and entirely pathetic. "I thought we could have a drink, look at the water, and talk like human beings."

"I don't drink at eleven on a Tuesday," Meredith said.

She slid the spreadsheet into her portfolio, zipped it shut, and stood. Above Q’s reclined figure, she looked vertical and solid—a person with bones and weight and a train to catch, while he remained horizontal, soft against his striped towel.

"I'll wait for the HR letter," she said. "Don't get up. You don't have your shoes on."

She walked toward the pavilion, her loafers clicking briskly against the decking until the sound was swallowed by the filtration system.

For a long time, Q didn't move. He stared at the concrete between his feet. Slowly, he leaned back and laid his forearm across his eyes, the way children do when pretending to be asleep so their parents won't make them clean their rooms. He let out a shuddering sigh.

Minutes later, Arthur emerged from the pool, toweling his shins. "Ready for lunch?" he asked. "They do a fluke crudo that justifies the initiation fee."

"Sure," I said.

I stood, leaving the biography behind, and adjusted my hat. Stepping out from behind the planter, my shadow fell briefly across Q’s legs. He didn't lower his arm, and I didn't say his name. I just walked past him into the glare of the deck, feeling an odd buoyancy—not cruelty, and certainly not triumph, but the quiet, vast relief of discovering that gravity on Earth was uniform after all.
